blocks.title: Writing Cubic Functions from Intercepts

legend.meaning: leading coefficient; found using an extra point

rows.1: Identify the three $ x $-intercepts: $ r_1, r_2, r_3 $.
Write $ f(x) = a(x - r_1)(x - r_2)(x - r_3) $.
Pick a fourth point $ (x_0, y_0) $ on the graph.
Substitute $ x_0 $ and $ y_0 $ and solve for $ a $.
Write the final function and check end behavior.

visuals.title: Steps to Write a Cubic from Its Graph

explanation: Two points determine a line (linear), three points determine a parabola (quadratic), and four points not on a line or parabola determine a [[kw:cubic function]].
If you know the three $ x $-intercepts of a cubic, write the factored form: $$ f(x) = a(x - r_1)(x - r_2)(x - r_3) $$
To find the leading coefficient $ a $, substitute the coordinates of a fourth point on the graph (not an intercept).
Solve for $ a $ and then you can expand to standard form if needed.
Always check the end behavior to make sure the sign of $ a $ matches the graph.

confusionCorner.title: Signs in Factored Form
confusionCorner.body: Remember: an $ x $-intercept of $ -4 $ gives the factor $ (x - (-4)) = (x + 4) $. [[imp:Watch the signs carefully when writing factors!]]

examples.prompt: The graph of a cubic function has $ x $-intercepts at $ -4, 1, 3 $ and passes through $ (0, -6) $. Write the function.
steps: Factored form: $ f(x) = a(x + 4)(x - 1)(x - 3) $.
Solve: $ a = -\frac{1}{2} $.
The function is $ f(x) = -\frac{1}{2}(x+4)(x-1)(x-3) $.
examples.title: Example A — Finding $ a $ from a Fourth Point

examples.prompt: Why can't we determine a cubic function uniquely from only its three $ x $-intercepts?
examples.title: Example B — Why a Fourth Point?
steps: Many different cubics can cross the $ x $-axis at the same three places if they are stretched vertically by different factors or reflected.
The leading coefficient $ a $ controls the vertical stretch and whether the graph opens upward or downward.
Without a fourth point, $ a $ can be any nonzero number, giving infinitely many curves.
The extra point pins down the exact value of $ a $.

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine you have a set of data points equally spaced in $ x $. By repeatedly subtracting consecutive $ y $-values, you can uncover the exact degree of the polynomial that fits the data—like a secret code hidden in the numbers.

examples.prompt: The table shows $ (1,1), (2,4), (3,10), (4,20), (5,35), (6,56), (7,84) $. Find the degree of the polynomial that fits this data exactly.
steps: 1st differences: $ 3,6,10,15,21,28 $ (not constant).
2nd differences: $ 3,4,5,6,7 $ (not constant).
3rd differences: $ 1,1,1,1 $ (constant!).
Third differences constant → cubic polynomial (degree 3).
examples.title: Example A — Determine Degree from Differences

examples.peerPrompt:

Discuss with a partner: Take $ f(x)=x^2 $. Compute $ f(x+1)-f(x) $ and then again. What happens to the $ x^2 $ term?
examples.title: Example B — Why Constant $ n $th Differences?
steps: The second difference: $ (2(x+1)+1) - (2x+1) = 2 $, constant.
Each subtraction reduces the degree by 1, so after $ n $ subtractions, an $ n $th-degree polynomial becomes constant.
examples.prompt: Explain why a quadratic function ($ x^2 $) has constant second differences.

steps: First differences: $ 9,7,-1,-15,-35 $ (not constant).
Second differences: $ -2,-8,-14,-20 $ (not constant).
Third differences: $ -6,-6,-6 $ (constant).
Degree 3 (cubic).
examples.title: Example C — Using Differences to Find Degree

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If } n\text{th differences are constant } \neq 0, \text{ then degree } = n. $$

legend.meaning: the differences don't change from row to row

explanation: [[kw:Finite differences]] are found by subtracting consecutive $ y $-values when the $ x $-values are equally spaced.
If the first differences are constant, the data fits a linear model (degree 1).
If the second differences are constant, the data fits a quadratic model (degree 2).
In general, if the $ n $th differences are nonzero and constant, the data can be modeled exactly by a polynomial of degree $ n $.
Once you know the degree, you can use regression (calculator) to find the exact polynomial coefficients.

confusionCorner.title: Equally Spaced $ x $-Values Are Key
confusionCorner.body: Finite differences only work when the $ x $-values are [[imp:equally spaced]]. If the spacing is uneven, you cannot use this method directly.

blocks.title: Finite Differences and Polynomial Degree

confusionCorner.body: Polynomial models are reliable only within or near the range of the given data. Predicting far outside that range (extrapolation) can give absurd results because polynomials grow rapidly.

examples.title: Example B — Interpreting $ R^2 $
steps: $ R^2 $ measures how closely the model's predicted values match the actual data. A value of 1 means perfect fit.
$ R^2 = 0.99 $ means the model explains 99% of the variation in the data; only 1% is due to other factors or randomness.
High $ R^2 $ gives confidence in predictions made with the model.

discoveryHook.scenario: Real-world data rarely follows a perfect polynomial. But with regression technology, we can find the best-fitting cubic (or quartic) model to make predictions—just like scientists forecasting energy use or population growth.

explanation: When data do not fit exactly, use a graphing calculator or software to perform [[kw:polynomial regression]].
Steps: 1) Enter data into lists. 2) Make a scatter plot to see the shape. 3) Choose a polynomial degree (often cubic or quartic). 4) Use regression to find coefficients.
The calculator gives the polynomial and a value $ R^2 $ (coefficient of determination). The closer $ R^2 $ is to 1, the better the fit.
After obtaining the model, graph it over the scatter plot to visually check, then use the model to predict other values.
Cubic regression gives a model of the form $$ y = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d $$

blocks.title: Combining Finite Differences and Regression

explanation: Step 1: Check if $ x $-values are equally spaced. If so, compute finite differences to determine the likely degree of the polynomial model.
Step 2: Use a graphing calculator to perform polynomial regression of that degree (or nearby degrees) and compare $ R^2 $ values.
Step 3: Choose the simplest model (lowest degree) that fits well. A high $ R^2 $ with a lower degree is usually better than a slightly higher $ R^2 $ with a higher degree.
Step 4: Use the model to make predictions within the data range.
Real data may not have exact constant differences, but the order where they become nearly constant suggests the degree.

rows.1: Higher-degree polynomial regression (but be careful of overfitting)

teacherCues: Ask: If you have a table of equally spaced data, what should you check first?
Show how finite differences suggest the degree, then regression finds the exact model.

steps: $ x $-values are not equally spaced (1,2,4,6,7,8), so finite differences won't work directly. Use regression.
Scatter plot suggests a gentle curve. Try quadratic and cubic regressions.
Quadratic might fit well with a high $ R^2 $. (Actual regression gives something like $ y = -0.5x^2 + 7.5x + 8 $.)
Choose the simplest model with strong $ R^2 $.

examples.title: Example B — Why Not Always Higher Degree?
steps: A high-degree polynomial will wiggle to pass exactly through all points, but it may swing wildly between them, giving terrible predictions.
This is called overfitting. A simpler model captures the trend without the noise.
Lower-degree polynomials are smoother and usually more reliable.
First differences are nearly constant (around 5). Second differences are close to zero.
A linear model would fit very well; a quadratic is unnecessary.
So choose linear.

examples.title: Example B — Checking Reasonableness
examples.prompt: Why is it important to check if a prediction makes sense in context?
steps: Real-world quantities like energy use cannot be negative. If the model predicts negative, it's a sign that the model is not valid outside the data range.
Always compare the predicted value to the trend; a sudden jump or drop indicates overfitting or a bad model choice.
Skepticism of extrapolation is healthy.

confusionCorner.body: The regression equation is an approximation. Predictions are estimates, not exact values. Always report predictions with appropriate rounding and mention that they are approximate.
confusionCorner.title: Regression Doesn't Give Exact Answers
